questions.q: Which gives the name of this alcohol and its classification?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula: a five-carbon chain with an OH group on the middle carbon.

questions.solution: The chain has five carbons with the OH group on carbon 3, whichever end is numbered from: pentan-3-ol. The carbon carrying the OH is bonded to two other carbons, so the alcohol is secondary. (Counting the carbons in the whole molecule, rather than those bonded to the C–OH carbon, leads to tertiary.)

questions.q: Which alcohol is not oxidised when warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
questions.solution: 2-methylpropan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol: the carbon carrying its OH group has no hydrogen atom, so it is not easily oxidised and the dichromate stays orange. The other three are primary or secondary. (2-methylpropan-1-ol is branched, but it is primary.)

questions.q: Ethanol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Which describes the colour change and its cause?

options.A: Orange to green: dichromate(VI) ions are reduced to chromium(III) ions
options.B: Orange to green: the organic product is green
options.C: Green to orange: chromium(III) ions are oxidised to dichromate(VI) ions
options.D: Purple to colourless: manganate(VII) ions are reduced

questions.solution: The alcohol is oxidised, and the orange \(\mathrm{Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}}\) ions are reduced to green \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) ions. The organic products, ethanal and ethanoic acid, are colourless. (Purple to colourless is the change for manganate(VII).)

questions.q: Propan-1-ol is oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Which method gives propanal as the main product?

options.A: Heat under reflux with an excess of the oxidising agent
options.B: Heat under reflux for an hour, then distil
options.C: Heat gently and distil off the propanal as soon as it forms
options.D: Leave the mixture at room temperature for a week

questions.solution: Propanal is easily oxidised further to propanoic acid. Distilling it off as it forms removes it from the oxidising agent, so the aldehyde is collected. Heating under reflux, especially with excess oxidant, keeps the aldehyde in the flask until it becomes the carboxylic acid. (Reflux is the method for the acid, not the aldehyde.)

questions.q: This alcohol is heated under reflux with an excess of acidified potassium dichromate(VI). What is the organic product?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula: a four-carbon chain with an OH group on the second carbon.

questions.solution: The alcohol is butan-2-ol, a secondary alcohol, so it is oxidised to a ketone, butanone. A ketone is not oxidised further, so even with excess oxidant under reflux no carboxylic acid forms. (Butanal and butanoic acid come from butan-1-ol, a primary alcohol.)

questions.q: Which equation, using [O] for the oxidising agent, shows the oxidation of ethanol to ethanoic acid?
questions.solution: Ethanol, \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}O}\), becomes ethanoic acid, \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}O_{2}}\): it gains one O and loses two H. The two H leave as water with a second O, so two [O] are needed: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}OH + 2[O] \rightarrow CH_{3}COOH + H_{2}O}\). (The equation giving \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CHO}\) is correct but shows oxidation only as far as the aldehyde.)

questions.q: Which reagent and conditions carry out this conversion?

figure.alt: Reaction scheme: cyclohexanol is converted into cyclohexene. A question mark stands over the arrow in place of the reagent and conditions.

options.B: Heat under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide
options.D: Heat with hydrogen and a nickel catalyst

questions.solution: The conversion removes water from the alcohol, a dehydration (elimination). It is done by heating with an acid catalyst, concentrated phosphoric acid (or concentrated sulfuric acid), and distilling off the cyclohexene. (Acidified dichromate would oxidise cyclohexanol to cyclohexanone.)

questions.q: In the acid-catalysed dehydration of propan-2-ol, the protonated alcohol loses a water molecule. Which species forms?
questions.solution: The OH group first takes an \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) from the acid. The C–O bond then breaks heterolytically, both electrons going with the water molecule, so the carbon that held the OH becomes positive: \(\mathrm{(CH_{3})_{2}CH^{+}}\), a secondary carbocation. It then loses \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) from a neighbouring carbon to give propene. (The charge stays on the carbon that carried the OH, so no primary carbocation forms.)

questions.q: Which alcohol gives only one alkene on dehydration, with no stereoisomers?
questions.solution: From 2-methylpropan-2-ol, H can be lost from any of the three identical methyl groups, so the only product is 2-methylpropene, which has no E/Z isomers. Pentan-3-ol gives only pent-2-ene, but as E and Z isomers; butan-2-ol and pentan-2-ol each give three alkenes. (Forgetting E/Z isomers makes pentan-3-ol look right.)

questions.q: Which conditions are used to make ethanol by fermentation of glucose?

options.A: Yeast in aqueous solution at about 35 °C, with air bubbled through
options.B: Yeast in aqueous solution at about 35 °C, with air kept out
options.C: Yeast in aqueous solution at about 80 °C, with air kept out
options.D: A phosphoric acid catalyst at about 300 °C and 60 atm

questions.solution: Enzymes in yeast catalyse the reaction. About 35 °C is warm enough for a reasonable rate without denaturing the enzymes, and air is kept out so the yeast respires anaerobically and ethanol is not oxidised to ethanoic acid. (300 °C and 60 atm are the conditions for hydrating ethene.)

questions.q: Bioethanol from sugar cane is sometimes called carbon neutral. Why is it not truly carbon neutral?

options.A: Burning ethanol releases more carbon dioxide than the plants absorbed while growing
options.B: Fermentation releases carbon dioxide, which the plants never absorbed
options.C: Ethanol burns only incompletely, forming carbon monoxide
options.D: Energy, often from fossil fuels, is used to grow, harvest and transport the crop and to distil the ethanol

questions.solution: The carbon dioxide released by fermentation and combustion equals the carbon dioxide the crop absorbed by photosynthesis: six molecules in each case. But farming, making fertiliser, transport and distillation use energy, usually from fossil fuels, which adds carbon dioxide. (The equations themselves do balance: that is what the carbon-neutral claim rests on.)

questions.q: 4.60 g of ethanol (\(M_{\text{r}} = 46.0\)) is oxidised to ethanoic acid (\(M_{\text{r}} = 60.0\)). 3.90 g of pure ethanoic acid is collected. What is the percentage yield?
questions.solution: Moles of ethanol = \(\frac{4.60}{46.0}\) = 0.100 mol, so at most 0.100 mol of ethanoic acid can form: 0.100 × 60.0 = 6.00 g. Percentage yield = \(\frac{3.90}{6.00} \times 100\) = 65.0%. (Comparing 3.90 g with the 4.60 g of ethanol leads to 84.8%.)

questions.q: Solid phosphorus(V) chloride is added to dry ethanol. What is seen?

options.A: Effervescence of a gas that turns limewater milky
options.C: Steamy fumes, which turn damp blue litmus paper red
options.D: The mixture turns from orange to green

questions.solution: \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH + PCl_{5} \rightarrow C_{2}H_{5}Cl + POCl_{3} + HCl}\). The hydrogen chloride produced forms steamy (misty) fumes in moist air, and it is acidic, so it turns damp blue litmus red. (Fizzing with a gas that turns limewater milky is the test for a carboxylic acid with a carbonate.)

options.A: Potassium bromide and 50% concentrated sulfuric acid, heated
options.C: Aqueous potassium bromide on its own, heated under reflux

questions.solution: Potassium bromide and the acid react in the flask to form hydrogen bromide, which substitutes Br for the OH group of the alcohol. The acid is diluted to about 50% so that it does not oxidise the bromide ions to bromine. (Bromide ions on their own cannot replace an OH group.)

questions.q: How many moles of oxygen, \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\), are needed for the complete combustion of 1 mol of propan-1-ol, \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{7}OH}\)?
questions.solution: \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{7}OH + 4\tfrac{1}{2}O_{2} \rightarrow 3CO_{2} + 4H_{2}O}\). The products contain 6 + 4 = 10 oxygen atoms; the alcohol supplies 1, so 9 must come from \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\), which is 4.5 mol. (Forgetting the oxygen atom in the alcohol leads to 5.0.)

questions.q: This shows part of the mechanism for the acid-catalysed hydration of ethene. In the second step, which species acts as the nucleophile?

figure.alt: Mechanism diagram: ethene and an H+ ion, with a curly arrow from the C=C bond to the H+. The carbocation formed is then attacked by a water molecule, with a curly arrow from a lone pair on its oxygen to the positive carbon.

questions.solution: In the second step a lone pair on the oxygen of a water molecule forms a bond to the positive carbon of the carbocation, so water is the electron pair donor: the nucleophile. \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) is the electrophile in the first step, and the carbocation is an electrophile too. (The product loses \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) to give ethanol, regenerating the catalyst.)
